profile.summary: xTrimoPGLM is a family of protein language models that handles both understanding and generation. One pretraining framework combines a masked (autoencoding) objective with an autoregressive one, so the same design yields masked models that embed and classify sequences and causal models that write new ones. The published family runs from 1 billion to 100 billion parameters, the largest trained on 1 trillion tokens. A masked model takes an amino acid sequence and returns per-residue embeddings or mask predictions; a causal model continues a sequence prompt.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README.md: Introduction to xTrimoPGLM Family Models

summary_quotes.text: We propose a unified protein language model, xTrimoPGLM, to address these two types of tasks simultaneously through an innovative pretraining framework.
a strategy for training xTrimoPGLM at an unprecedented scale of 100 billion parameters and 1 trillion training tokens
xTrimoPGLM is the open-source version of the latest protein language models towards protein understanding tasks (Masked Protein Language Models) and protein design (Casual Protein Language Models).

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The family is built on the GLM transformer design, as the ProteinGLM model and config classes show: the released 1B masked model has 24 layers, hidden size 2048, 32 attention heads and a vocabulary of 128 tokens. The contribution the paper claims is joint optimisation of two pretraining objectives, autoencoding and autoregressive, in one model. In the released code a single configuration flag, is_causal, switches a checkpoint between masked use and causal use, and the loading class decides whether the output is mask predictions, a sequence label, per-token labels or generated text.

quotes.text: most existing models are limited by either autoencoding or autoregressive pretraining objectives, which makes them struggle to handle protein understanding and generation tasks concurrently
an exploration of the compatibility and the potential for joint optimization of the two types of objectives

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README lists seven downloads: 1B, 3B and 10B masked models, 1B, 3B and 7B causal models, and the int4 quantised 100B model that serves both uses. When read on 26 November 2026, the three masked repositories and the int4 100B repository answered, each redirected to a proteinglm name (for example xtrimopglm-1b-mlm answers as proteinglm-1b-mlm), and the model card is titled ProteinPGLM-1B-MLM and credits Tsinghua University alone. The Hugging Face API returned the error 'Invalid username or password.' for the three causal repositories on 26 November 2026. A result must name the size, the objective and the Hugging Face revision, because the naming has changed since the paper.

sections.title: What the developers report
sections.body: The README reports out-of-distribution perplexity on two held-out sets of about 10,000 sequences each, one below 0.9 and one below 0.5 sequence identity to the training data, and compares with ESM2 and ProGen2-xlarge. The developers' own figures put the masked 1B model behind ESM2 3B (9.3 against 7.7 on the set below 0.9 identity) and the 100B model ahead of both (6.7). The paper's abstract claims better results than other baselines on 18 protein understanding benchmarks. These are the developers' claims and have not been reproduced by Rewire.

quotes.text: xTrimoPGLM is the open-source version of the latest protein language models towards protein understanding tasks (Masked Protein Language Models) and protein design (Casual Protein Language Models).

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: GLM transformer. The 1B masked checkpoint has 24 layers, hidden size 2048, 32 attention heads and a 128 token vocabulary; the is_causal flag selects masked or causal use.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: An amino acid sequence, tokenised one residue at a time. A causal model takes a sequence prefix as a prompt, including the empty prompt.

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: Masked models give per-residue hidden states, and with the classification heads a sequence-level or per-token prediction. Causal models generate a sequence from a prompt.

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: 1,209,144,048 (1B MLM); 2,834,612,736 (3B MLM); 10,686,572,816 (10B MLM); 50,227,927,296 tensor entries for the int4 100B file. The causal 1B, 3B and 7B models are listed in the README but their repositories did not answer.

run_guide.summary: Load the 1B masked checkpoint and get per-residue embeddings for one sequence.
prerequisites: Python with transformers and torch; the loader needs trust_remote_code because the model class ships with the checkpoint.
A CUDA GPU: the example moves the model and the inputs to the GPU. For the int4 100B model the README states a single A100 or A800 with 80GB.
The code and the weights are CC BY-NC 4.0, so non-commercial use only.

steps.title: Install the Python packages
steps.explanation: The README's example imports transformers and torch, and names accelerate for the dispatch load path. Rewire wrote the pip line; the sources name the packages but give no install command.

quotes.text:
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoModelForTokenClassification, AutoTokenizer, AutoConfig
import torch

steps.title: Get residue embeddings from the 1B masked model
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer
import torch

tokenizer  = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Bo1015/proteinglm-1b-mlm", trust_remote_code=True, use_fast=True)
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("Bo1015/proteinglm-1b-mlm",  trust_remote_code=True, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16)
if torch.cuda.is_available():
    model = model.cuda()
model.eval()

seq = 'MILMCQHFSGQFSKYFLAVSSDFCHFVFPIILVSHVNFKQMKRKGFALWNDRAVPFTQGIFTTVMILLQYLHGTG'
output = tokenizer(seq, add_special_tokens=True, return_tensors='pt')
with torch.inference_mode():
    inputs = {"input_ids": output["input_ids"].cuda(), "attention_mask": output["attention_mask"].cuda()}
    output_embeddings = model(**inputs, output_hidden_states=True, return_last_hidden_state=True).hidden_states[:-1, 0] # get rid of the <eos> token
print(output_embeddings.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: Copied from the model card's How to use block, which loads Bo1015/proteinglm-1b-mlm. Rewire wrapped it in a shell heredoc and added the final print so the step shows a result. The repository README runs the same code against biomap-research/xtrimopglm-100b-int4, which needs an 80GB GPU.

steps.title: Generate a sequence with a causal model
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, AutoConfig
import torch

tokenizer  = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("biomap-research/xtrimopglm-100b-int4", trust_remote_code=True, use_fast=True)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained("biomap-research/xtrimopglm-100b-int4",  trust_remote_code=True, torch_dtype=torch.half)
config.is_causal=True
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("biomap-research/xtrimopglm-100b-int4", config = config, torch_dtype=torch.half,trust_remote_code=True)
if torch.cuda.is_available():
    model = model.cuda()
model.eval()

gen_kwargs = {'max_length': 256, 'top_p': 0.8, 'temperature':0.9, "num_beams": 1}
prompt=['', 'MLFVVL', 'LDL', 'VTQA']

for idx, each in enumerate(prompt):
    print(f"Begin generating idx: {idx} with prompt {each}")
    output = model.chat(tokenizer, each, **gen_kwargs)
    print(f"\nEnd generation with length: {len(output.split())} - seqs: {output}\n")
PY

notes: Three things for a reviewer. First, the Hugging Face naming: every xtrimopglm path that answered redirects to a proteinglm repository, the 1B card is titled ProteinPGLM-1B-MLM and credits Tsinghua University alone, and its own usage block loads Bo1015/proteinglm-1b-mlm, a third account the README does not mention. This model record may overlap a ProteinGLM record. Second, for the three causal repositories (1B, 3B, 7B CLM) the Hugging Face API returned the error 'Invalid username or password.' on 26 November 2026; the saved hf-api-1b-clm.json holds that response and the structured rows for them carry nulls. Third, the paper (Nature Methods) is not open access, so only the Europe PMC abstract was read; the training corpus is unnamed in every file read. The int4 100B parameter figure is the count of tensor entries the API reports (22,108,416 in F32 plus 50,205,818,880 in I8), not a count of distinct trained parameters at full precision.
